newsitem.title: DUBAI: Thai warrant is Khashoggi's latest legal wrangle.
newsitem.headline: Thai warrant is Khashoggi's latest legal wrangle.

text.p: Thailand's issue of an arrest warrant for Saudi Arabian tycoon Adnan Khashoggi is the most recent legal tussle dogging the jetsetting financier who was once one of the world's richest men.
Thai police said on Friday they had issued arrest warrants for Khashoggi and four other officials of the Bangkok Bank of Commerce Plc (BBC) on charges of conspiring to defraud the bank.

An officer said the Bank of Thailand requested the warrants for the five on suspicion that they jointly conspired for Khashoggi, 61, to draw two billion baht ($77.5 million) in loans from the BBC without credible collateral in 1995.
The whereabouts of the globetrotting businessman are unknown. But his multi-million dollar deals, court cases and elite acquaintances have spread his fame throughout the world.
Khashoggi, whose wealth once totalled $4 billion, amassed one of the largest personal fortunes in the world by playing middleman in the transfer of Western arms and technology to Arab oil states.
Much of it came from commissions paid in the 1970s by Western corporations that he guided in dealing with an Arab world flush with petrodollars and anxious to modernise.
In 1986 Khashoggi played a key role in initiating contacts between Israel and U.S. officials on the American government's then-secret scheme to sell arms to Iran.
The son of the personal physician to the late King Abdul-Aziz ibn Saud, Khashoggi was born on July 25, 1935.

Throughout his career, he hobnobbed with the high and mighty, entertaining the likes of former U.S. secretary of state Henry Kissinger, former head of Chrysler Corp Lee Iacocca and King Juan Carlos of Spain on his private yacht.
Khashoggi housed former Haitian dictator Jean-Claude "Baby Doc" Duvalier at his Riviera villa for years after he was deposed in 1986.
In the 1990s, the Saudi entrepreneur's legal battles made him a household name.

In mid-1990, a U.S. federal court cleared Khashoggi of obstruction of justice and mail fraud charges for allegedly helping former Philippine first lady Imelda Marcos conceal ownership of New York real estate and art that was allegedly bought with funds stolen from the Philippines.
A week later the U.S. government dropped racketeering charges against him.
But in November 1991, the small and plump businessman, who has owned homes from Europe to Manhattan and Riyadh, lost a U.S. Supreme Court appeal of a $4.6 million default judgment against him.

The judgment had stemmed from a dispute between Khashoggi and the National Development Co. of the Philippines over the dissolving of a joint venture. In the dispute, the firm claimed Khashoggi improperly converted millions of dollars of the joint ventures assets.
Khashoggi's business interests have ranged from media and tourism to cement, semiconductors and pipes.
